title: Running Away from Running Records
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos, a primary classroom teacher, argues that traditional running records, with their meaning, structure and visual (M/S/V) miscue analysis, are no longer worth the instructional time they consume. She frames the case through opportunity costs, citing Mark Seidenberg on the time that over-teaching eats, and stacks up critiques from Rachael Gabriel, Timothy Shanahan, Alison Clarke, Anna Geiger and Jocelyn Seamer, along with a Review of Educational Research systematic review of the evidence. Responding to whole language professor Andy Johnson's defense of the tool, she walks through his sample miscues and shows that nearly every error points to a decoding gap, so categorizing which errors make sense adds little actionable information. Her alternative is simply listening to students read and informally assessing decoding and language comprehension, in line with the simple view of reading. She closes with the claim that teacher expertise shows up in learner progress and that the running record has run its course.
points: Janetos casts the running record debate as one of opportunity cost: every minute spent coding miscues is a minute not spent advancing reading and writing.
Her walk through Andy Johnson's own sample shows the errors were decoding failures, so analyzing which ones preserved meaning adds no instructional direction.
She argues that for beginning readers the useful question is only whether word recognition is accurate, which echoes the orthographic mapping and self-teaching literature she cites.
The review evidence and a chorus of literacy specialists converge on the point that M/S/V analysis is subjective, slow and lacks a validated instructional protocol.

In place of a form, she keeps listening to students read often and informally checks decoding and language comprehension, treating teacher expertise as learner progress rather than visible performance.
quotes: It’s not because Halloween was only a few days ago that I say this passage haunts me. In fact, opportunity costs are my constant companions as I ask myself: How important is what I’m doing right now? Is it keeping me from advancing the primary goals of reading and writing?
Let’s go cot a bin fish is a great example of how inaccurate decoding can impede comprehension.

All reading should be meaningful, and if you can’t read the words, it’s very difficult—often impossible—to make meaning, as we’ve just seen in this running record. My task is to fill the phonics gaps and provide plenty of opportunities to practice reading connected text.

The M/S/V analysis in traditional running records simply isn’t the most efficient way to ascertain a reading profile for my beginning readers to accurately assess their progress as research by Matthew Burns has shown.

I’d recommend against evaluating oral reading errors – the useless efforts to determine their orthographic-phonetic, syntactic, semantic accuracy. There will be serious reliability problems with such analyses – and there is no validated instructional protocol based on differentiated responses to these.

Those who are not currently in charge of a classroom full of kids sometimes forget the time it takes to address the social, emotional, and academic needs of these children and how the instructional choices we make reflect conscious decisions to include some activities and exclude others.

The outsider’s recommendation can quickly become the insider’s reckoning with the unforgiving clock. We’re not just clocking hours in the classroom until the dismissal bell rings; we’re maximizing each and every minute and doing a cost/benefit analysis of the lessons we teach.
